node.label: Bruce Curtis
node.date_label: With Corrigan, “Education, Inspection and State Formation” 1985 · Building the Educational State 1988 · True Government by Choice Men? 1992 · The Politics of Population 2001 · “After ‘Canada’” 2009 · Ruling by Schooling Quebec 2012
node.description: A historical sociologist (Carleton University) whose studies of schooling, school inspection and the census in the Canadas read administration as a means of rule. In Building the Educational State (1988), as a reviewer quotes it, education 'was not a means to government; education was government: government of the self' (p. 110), and the educational state was built 'only through the destruction of a prior educational organization' (p. 15); in True Government by Choice Men? (1992) 'Educational inspection was about state formation: the creation, stabilization and normalisation of relations of power, authority, domination and exploitation' (p. 32). His census history (2001) holds that 'Census making ... is not in any simple sense the taking of things as they are; in an important sense it is the making of things to be taken' (p. 305, as Belshaw quotes it), and in a 1996 review he wrote that 'The census simply cannot tell us much about the value of distributed property, about the gendered distribution of property, certainly nothing about inheritance patterns'. Reviewers credited his joining of Foucault's analysis of power to a Marxist theory of state formation but found gender relations missing (Davey 1989; Miller 1993), and Bryan Palmer judged the inspection study, taken as a model, 'overstated to the point of distorting actual historical relations in the evolution of state and civil society' (1993). In the debate over Ian McKay's liberal order framework, Nancy Christie cites 'Bruce Curtis's important point that what McKay is really describing is governmentality' (2009).
node.representative_figures_and_works: Bruce Curtis (b. 1950); with Philip Corrigan, “Education, Inspection and State Formation: A Preliminary Statement” (CHA Historical Papers, 1985); Building the Educational State: Canada West, 1836–1871 (1988); True Government by Choice Men? Inspection, Education, and State Formation in Canada West (1992); The Politics of Population: State Formation, Statistics, and the Census of Canada, 1840–1875 (2001); “After ‘Canada’: Liberalisms, Social Theory, and Historical Analysis” (2009); Ruling by Schooling Quebec: Conquest to Liberal Governmentality – A Historical Sociology (2012).
node.scope_note: This entry presents Curtis's state-formation studies of schooling, inspection and the census (1985–2001) and their place in the liberal order debate. Read on 2026-10-14: his review of Darroch and Soltow (1996, pp. 107–110) in full, and four in-period or near-period reviews of his books in full: Davey (1989) on Building the Educational State, Miller (1993) and Palmer (1993) on True Government by Choice Men?, and Belshaw (2002) on The Politics of Population; Christie (2009) was re-read for its Curtis passage. His books are unread: his words from them are reviewers' quotations, with the reviewers' page references. The 1985 article with Corrigan, the 2009 chapter and Ruling by Schooling Quebec (2012) are title- or summary-level only. He is a sociologist, not a historian by department; the atlas's moral regulation entry treats his state-formation work as shared ground with the liberal order framework, not membership.

incident_edges.relationship: Schooling, school inspection and the census studied as state formation in the Canadas: education as 'government of the self' (1988), inspection as the making of 'relations of power, authority, domination and exploitation' (1992), the census as 'the making of things to be taken' (2001); work that predates the framework, and that Christie later cites for the point that McKay describes governmentality (2009)
incident_edges.evidence_note: In-period reviews, read in full; Curtis's books are unread, so his words are the reviewers' quotations with their page references. Davey (Historical Studies in Education 1, 1989, pp. 161–165) on Building the Educational State (1988): 'one of the great strengths of Curtis' approach is his grounding of Foucault's analysis of power and subjectivity within a marxist theory of state formation and cultural forms' (p. 161); he quotes Curtis that 'the construction of the Educational State was accomplished only through the destruction of a prior educational organization and the marginalization of the structure of educational possibilities' (book p. 15), that schooling meant 'the anchoring of the conditions of political governance in the selves of the governed' (no page given), that education 'was not a means to government; education was government: government of the self' (book p. 110) and that 'public education was administered into dominance only through a myriad of local struggles' (book p. 132); Davey notes 'there is no reference to Gramsci or the theory of hegemony in the bibliography or the index' (p. 162) and objects that Curtis 'fails to provide an adequate account of patriarchal relations in the period' (p. 165). Miller (Historical Studies in Education 5, 1993, pp. 123–126) on True Government by Choice Men? (1992) quotes 'Educational inspection was about state formation: the creation, stabilization and normalisation of relations of power, authority, domination and exploitation' (book p. 32) and 'Bureaucratic administration was seen by political liberals as practical education, a ‘normal school’ for the people' (book p. 7); she says Curtis 'carefully distances himself' from a social-control argument (p. 124) and regrets 'the relative invisibility of gender relations' (p. 125). Bryan Palmer (Labour/Le Travail 31, 1993, pp. 365–367): 'In their purpose they can only be applauded; but their search is at times disturbingly narrow' (p. 365); as a 'model' Curtis's account 'is overstated to the point of distorting actual historical relations in the evolution of state and civil society' (p. 366); yet he credits Curtis and Colonial Leviathan with 'the notion that the coming of ‘responsible government’ actually entailed the subversion of the reform strategy of the 1830s' (p. 366). Later readings: Belshaw (2002, read) quotes the census book: 'Census making ... is not in any simple sense the taking of things as they are; in an important sense it is the making of things to be taken' (book p. 305). Christie (Underhill Review 2009, read): 'Here I think we need to be alert to Bruce Curtis's important point that what McKay is really describing is governmentality'; this is Christie's characterisation, and Curtis's own 2009 chapter ('After ‘Canada’') is unread. The edge records a contribution to the strand the atlas calls 'State formation before the framework'; the work predates McKay's prospectus (2000, unread beyond its abstract), and no checked text by McKay names Curtis. The collaboration with Philip Corrigan (1985) is title-level; the moral regulation entry treats this state-formation work as shared ground (edge_848), so no separate Curtis edge to moral_regulation is drawn.

incident_edges.relationship: Census returns read as artefacts of state knowledge rather than transparent records: objections to inferring property, gender and inheritance from the 1871 Ontario census in a review of Darroch and Soltow (1996), and census making as 'the making of things to be taken' (2001)
incident_edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents Curtis's 1996 review of Gordon Darroch and Lee Soltow's census study of property in Ontario (1994) and his census history (2001); it is not a verdict on quantitative history as a whole, and Darroch and Soltow are not in the atlas. His own words (Historical Studies in Education 8, 1996, pp. 107–110, read in full): 'Anyone who has worked with manuscript census data must be impressed with the meticulous and painstaking analysis undertaken here' (p. 109); 'Two related critical points seem worth making about census artifacts and the matter of gender' (p. 109); the authors 'go so far as to suggest that their cross-sectional study is actually longitudinal' (p. 109); 'The census simply cannot tell us much about the value of distributed property, about the gendered distribution of property, certainly nothing about inheritance patterns, although, as an ideological practice, census-taking attached property to adult men' (pp. 109–110); and, qualifying, 'the book is an important contribution to ongoing debates' (p. 110). The census book (2001) is unread; as Belshaw quotes it (2002, read), 'Census making ... is not in any simple sense the taking of things as they are; in an important sense it is the making of things to be taken' (book p. 305), and it 'seeks to tie individuals within an administrative grid and then to hold them steady so that they may become objects of knowledge and government' (book p. 26). Belshaw's reading, in his words: 'Historical demographers know that the census is far from perfectly reliable but, after reading Bruce Curtis’ latest book, many more will be mindful of how political it is throughout', and 'demographic and social historians may ignore Curtis’ findings at their peril'. Kind: critique, because the 1996 text objects to inferences drawn from census returns; it is not a rejection of quantitative work, and Curtis calls the book he reviews an important contribution.

named_group_routes.relationship: Canada as a project of liberal rule: the prospectus of 2000
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period evidence (2000). The prospectus abstract (read) proposes mapping 'the Canadian state as a project of liberal rule in northern North America' to get beyond the 'socio-cultural versus national-political impasse'. Its core formulation (pp. 620–21) is checked as quoted by Fecteau (2009): 'Canada-as-project can be analyzed through the study of the implantation and expansion over a heterogeneous terrain of a certain politico-economic logic – to wit liberalism.' The prospectus body is not read here. McKay's spring 2000 Acadiensis essay (pp. 90–91, read) sets out the same programme in his own words: 'a strategy of reconnaissance'; the project 'was the project of liberal order, a coherent attempt to install a liberal public philosophy and practice of "peace, order and good government" in northern North America'; 'Canada was thus a process, not a self-evident thing, and the key to this process was liberalization'. A contribution, not a founding: state-formation studies (Curtis 1988; Greer and Radforth 1992) precede it, and Pâquet (2009) names Gramsci and Fernande Roy (1988) as its sources. In the sampled corpus, 90 of 1,303 strict History doctoral dissertations dated 2009–2026 cite the prospectus. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. The 2009 reply and the histories of the left (2005, 2008) are later readings, not evidence for this edge.

named_group_routes.relationship: Liberalism read as a system of moral regulation and the liberal state as a constitutor of subjectivities (1991–92), beside the liberal order framework's later history of property, the individual and rule
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements, before McKay's prospectus (2000). 'Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State', Labour/Le Travail 30 (1992), pp. 213–222, read in full, endorses Mitchell Dean's argument 'that classical English liberalism was not a negation of state regulation but rather a particular system of economic, social, and moral regulation', so that 'a history of pauperism is also a genealogy of liberalism' (p. 217). She reviews Jean-Marie Fecteau's Un nouvel ordre des choses (1989) as 'a landmark work' whose 'theoretical sophistication' crosses 'the traditional historiographical boundaries separating coercion from benevolence and the state as a whole from charity' (pp. 221–222), but faults its 'moyens de contrôle' as 'a rather functionalist formulation', a 'model of negative class power', and adds that 'These moral codes are not intrinsic to the logic of capital, since capitalism works quite efficiently in different cultural systems' (p. 222). Note 10 (p. 220) cites Fecteau's essay in Greer and Radforth's Colonial Leviathan (1992), and the essay thanks Allan Greer for comments on a draft (p. 222). In the 1991 book (Google Books search-within snippets of the 2008 reissue, 1991 pagination) note 35 (p. 171) cites Bruce Curtis's 'Preconditions of the Canadian State', and she writes that moral regulation 'might be an important social process, which is intertwined with but is not an effect of either the economic or the political' (p. 165) and that 'one has to be sceptical of any claims that envision a clear separation between moral and economic regulation' (p. 166). Reviewers read the book's state argument in the same terms: private philanthropy 'allowed liberal democratic states to adhere to their policy of non-interference in the private sphere' (Loo 1992, p. 278, her paraphrase). Comparison only. The user decided (2026-10-12) that the liberal order framework is 'a different project closer to history of capitalism'; Fecteau and Curtis are shared ground (state formation), not membership. No in-period text by the framework's authors discussing her was read here (McKay's 2000 prospectus is paywalled and unread). edge_848 (liberal_order_framework – moral_regulation) is the field-level comparison. This edge is an editorial comparison of her 1992 argument with the later framework (McKay, 2000); she did not distinguish herself from a framework not yet formulated.

named_group_routes.relationship: Colonial Leviathan (1992, edited with Ian Radforth): mid-nineteenth-century state formation in the Canadas, written before the framework was named, and later faulted by Greer himself for neglecting Indigenous peoples (2019)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Colonial Leviathan is unread (lending-only copy; the Érudit, Left History and Histoire sociale reviews returned bot checks). In-period reading: Palmer (Labour/Le Travail 31, 1993, read in full) says the volume and Curtis's book 'are searching for the state in pre-Confederation Canada' (p. 365) and finds that 'the collection lacks coherence', while its 'single most important contribution ... also developed by Curtis, is the notion that the coming of ‘responsible government’ actually entailed the subversion of the reform strategy of the 1830s' (p. 366); he names Greer's chapter on the birth of the police (p. 366). Valverde's 1992 essay cites Fecteau's chapter in the volume (edge_966). Greer's own later judgment (2019, read): 'The time may be right, then, for a renewed history of the Confederation era, one that unites the history of state formation with that of settler colonialism' (p. 73), with n. 41: 'A prime example of this problem would be Colonial Leviathan; devoted to questions of state formation, it neglected everything to do with Indigenous peoples and processes of elimination' (p. 84). Comparison only: the volume predates McKay's prospectus (2000), and no checked text by McKay or his commentators names it; Pâquet (2009) links the framework to studies of state formation in general. The atlas's state_formation_roots strand places it there editorially.

sources.title: Ian McKay, "A Note on 'Region' in Writing the History of Atlantic Canada," Acadiensis 29, no. 2 (Spring 2000): 89–101.
sources.citation: Ian McKay, "A Note on 'Region' in Writing the History of Atlantic Canada," Acadiensis 29, no. 2 (Spring 2000): 89–101.

verification.note: Pages 89–90 read: a 1997 workshop programme dominated by gender, ethnicity and community rather than "regional underdevelopment, class conflict and the position of the Atlantic Provinces within Confederation"; this pluralism continues "the social-history revolution of the 1960s and 1970s" but "places a question mark over the very concept of an 'Atlantic Canada'". Checked against: UNB Libraries Acadiensis article page and PDF (citation line on p. 89). Addendum 2026-10-13: the whole essay (pp. 89–101) read in the UNB PDF. Note 1 (p. 89): 'a lightly-edited version of the introductory talk I prepared for the Atlantic Canada Workshop which met in Halifax in August 1997'. Pages 90–91 state the liberal-order programme: 'a strategy of reconnaissance'; 'That project, very briefly, was the project of liberal order, a coherent attempt to install a liberal public philosophy and practice of "peace, order and good government" in northern North America'; 'Canada was thus a process, not a self-evident thing, and the key to this process was liberalization'. Where region fits that approach: 'Quite centrally' (p. 95). The essay sets aside natural and essentialist definitions (pp. 95–96), asks heartland–hinterland and dependency models to 'undergo the rigorous analysis of concepts' (pp. 96–99) and resists a nationalizing historiography (p. 99). It proposes exploring 'the remarkable extent to which Atlantic Canadians built the Canadian liberal project' (p. 99) and the region's 'communitarian critique of the liberal order' (p. 100). Page 89 names 'the Gramscian assumptions that have shaped my outlook'.

sources.scope_note: A critique of region as a container for the new histories.

sources.title: Nancy Christie, “Revisiting Canada’s Project of Liberal Rule,” The Underhill Review (Carleton University), Fall 2009.
sources.citation: Nancy Christie, “Revisiting Canada’s Project of Liberal Rule,” The Underhill Review (Carleton University), Fall 2009.

verification.note: Text read: the framework gives coherence to a vast cultural and social literature; but McKay neglects republicanism, civic humanism and Ancien Régime sensibilities, over-emphasizes the state (Curtis: what McKay describes is "governmentality"), ignores religion as "a powerful vehicle in the creation of the liberal order", and his "definition of individualism based on property ownership" excludes women. Checked against: Carleton Underhill Review page read. Same work also checked as crr_christie_2009 (supporting_page_checked, 2026-10-12; cdn_religion_reform, cdn_religion_reform): Text read: no one acquainted with work by Fecteau, Hubert, Gauvreau and Christie on the Protestant churches and New Liberalism "can ignore religion as a powerful vehicle in the creation of the liberal order"; Catholic churches articulated modern liberal values of individualism and self-control. Checked against: Carleton Underhill Review page read. Addendum 2026-10-14: Re-read for the 1.139 Bruce Curtis person entry (Underhill Review web page, no pagination; the sixth paragraph of the essay by count): 'Here I think we need to be alert to Bruce Curtis's important point that what McKay is really describing is governmentality', 'a theoretical proposition which has the advantage of being much more precise and nuanced'. Christie names no Curtis work in that passage, and Curtis is not in her works-consulted list, so which text she means (presumably the 2009 chapter) is not established.

sources.scope_note: Critique and proposed extension: religion, voluntary associations, the family, gender.

sources.citation: Ian McKay, “The Liberal Order Framework: A Prospectus for a Reconnaissance of Canadian History,” Canadian Historical Review 81, no. 4 (December 2000): 617–45, doi:10.3138/chr.81.4.616.

verification.note: Abstract read: the way past the "socio-cultural versus national-political impasse" is a re/connaissance mapping the Canadian state as "a project of liberal rule in northern North America", through which "liberal order became the national-political ‘commonsense’". Article body unread; McKay’s phrases on liberty, equality and property and on keeping liberalism and capitalism analytically separate (p. 629) are known here only through Fecteau (2009). Page range revised 2026-10-12 (answers Q20): cite 617–45. The DOI begins at 616 (the abstract page); Project MUSE reportedly gives 616–645; Crossref and OpenAlex give 616–678, a metadata error (their CHR 81:4 ranges overlap). End page not yet checked against a PDF. The abstract does not define liberalism by liberty, equality and property: that trio is Fecteau's paraphrase, not a checked McKay quotation. The best checked opening formulation is McKay 2000, 620–1, as quoted by Fecteau ('a certain politico-economic logic – to wit liberalism'). The 'cannot be conflated' line on capitalism is from McKay's 2009 reply (p. 385), not this essay. Checked against: Crossref DOI record (CHR 81:4, December 2000; Crossref gives 616–678 for the forum span); OpenAlex abstract (English and French); page range 616–645 as cited by Parnaby (2019); Crossref journal listing for CHR 81:4 (https://api.crossref.org/journals/0008-3755/works?filter=from-pub-date:2000-12-01,until-pub-date:2000-12-31); Project MUSE record https://muse.jhu.edu/article/590654 (blocked; page range reported by search summary). Checked against: 49thshelf book page (first published April 1991, ISBN 9780771086892; UTP reissue June 2008); Crossref DOI record (UTP 2008); review in Labour/Le Travail 30 (1992), doi:10.2307/25143633. Same work also checked as crr_valverde_1991 (supporting_page_checked, 2026-10-12; cdn_religion_reform, cdn_religion_reform): Summary read: moral reform "was not the project of a marginal puritanical group but was central to the race, class, and gender organization of modern English Canada". Checked against: Open Library work OL1825719W; Crossref DOI of the 2008 reprint; OpenAlex summary. Addendum 2026-10-14: For the 1.135 person entry. The book's pages were not read. Wording is known from (a) in-period reviewers' quotations, read: Dehli 1992 (pp. 15, 17, 165), McCormick 1992 (pp. 9, 17, 42, 43, 90), Loo 1992 (pp. 35, 36, 41, 164), Wright 1995 (pp. 9–13, 41, 42, 43, 89–90, 98, 103, 166); and (b) Google Books search-within snippets of the 2008 UTP reissue (volume ghqEyXf5950C), whose page images were not viewable. The reissue keeps the 1991 pagination for the original text: the snippets put the reviewers' pp. 15, 17, 165 and 166 on the same pages, and the 1991 preface's p. 9 at p. ix (so 1991 p. 10 = 2008 p. x). Crossref chapter records: Preface ix–xiv; Introduction to the 2008 Edition 1–14; 1. Introduction 15–33; Notes 168–201. sources.title: Tina Loo, review of Mariana Valverde, The Age of Light, Soap and Water, Labour/Le Travail 30 (Fall 1992): 277–279.
sources.citation: Tina Loo, review of Mariana Valverde, The Age of Light, Soap and Water: Moral Reform in English Canada, 1885–1925 (Toronto, 1991), Labour/Le Travail 30 (Fall 1992): 277–279. doi:10.2307/25143633.

verification.note: Read in full in the journal's PDF of the issue's reviews section (lltjournal.ca article 4867, galley 5740; pp. 277–279; signed Tina Loo, Simon Fraser University). Crossref gives Labour/Le Travail 30, p. 277. Passages used: the book is 'not a history of events ... but one of meaning' (p. 277); the reformers' allegories taught 'the right type of consciousness' (p. 278, quoting p. 41); 'religion and sectarian differences' get 'rather short shrift'; Allen's typology; 'any discussion of the discourse of moral reform in Canada needs to address Christianity and certainly Protestantism more fully, even if only to dismiss its importance'; private philanthropy 'allowed liberal democratic states to adhere to their policy of non-interference in the private sphere' (p. 278, her paraphrase); the state argument 'seems to be more asserted than proved'; she 'locates her book in the separate, but converging disciplines of history and sociology'; 'a provocative and valuable contribution to the history of social reform and, more significantly, because of its self-conscious use of theory, to the writing of Canadian history' (p. 279).

sources.scope_note: In-period review by a historian (later co-author of Making Good, 1997).

sources.title: Mariana Valverde, “Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State,” Labour/Le Travail 30 (Fall 1992): 213–222.
sources.citation: Mariana Valverde, “Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State,” review essay on Mitchell Dean, The Constitution of Poverty (1991), Jean-Marie Fecteau, Un nouvel ordre des choses (1989), and Gertrude Himmelfarb, Poverty and Compassion (1991), Labour/Le Travail 30 (Fall 1992): 213–222.

verification.note: Read in full (pp. 213–222) in the journal's own PDF (lltjournal.ca article 4860, galley 5733; citation line on p. 213: Labour/Le Travail, 30 (Fall 1992), 213-22). Passages used: 'a critique of political economy for its failure to theorize moral regulation and subjectivity generally' (pp. 213–214); 'moral capital of the poor' (p. 215); 'the discourse of moral reform needs to be analyzed seriously, not merely dismissed as a cover for class interests' and 'moral discourse does as a matter of contingent fact legitimize certain class, gender, and racial interests' (p. 216); Dean shows 'that classical English liberalism was not a negation of state regulation but rather a particular system of economic, social, and moral regulation'; 'a history of pauperism is also a genealogy of liberalism'; Dean 'undercuts the Marxist view that moral regulation is an unimportant offshoot of economic class relations by expanding the analysis of the liberal state's role in constituting subjectivities pioneered by Corrigan and Sayer' (p. 217); Fecteau's study 'sadly lacking' Dean's awareness of gender (p. 220); n. 10 on Fecteau's essay in Colonial Leviathan and his perspective 'not to my knowledge otherwise represented in Canadian historiography' (p. 220); 'moyens de contrôle', 'a rather functionalist formulation', 'a model of negative class power', 'the pitfalls of marxist functionalism', 'These moral codes are not intrinsic to the logic of capital', 'a landmark work' (p. 222); thanks to Lynne Marks and Allan Greer (p. 222).

sources.scope_note: Her in-period statement of liberalism as moral regulation, and her critique of class-functionalist accounts of relief.

sources.title: John Douglas Belshaw, review of Bruce Curtis, The Politics of Population (2001), Historical Studies in Education / Revue d'histoire de l'éducation 14, no. 1 (2002): 122–125.
sources.citation: John Douglas Belshaw, review of Bruce Curtis, The Politics of Population: State Formation, Statistics, and the Census of Canada, 1840–1875 (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 2001), Historical Studies in Education / Revue d'histoire de l'éducation 14, no. 1 (2002): review section pp. 121–185.

verification.note: Read in full from the journal's own PDF (galley 2025; text layer). The running heads give pp. 123–125 for the second to fourth pages, so the review runs pp. 122–125; the OJS record gives first page 121 and last page 124. Review pages are therefore not used as locators; quotations of the book carry Belshaw's references to the book. Passages used: 'Historical demographers know that the census is far from perfectly reliable but, after reading Bruce Curtis’ latest book, many more will be mindful of how political it is throughout'; 'Census making ... is not in any simple sense the taking of things as they are; in an important sense it is the making of things to be taken' (book p. 305); census making 'seeks to tie individuals within an administrative grid and then to hold them steady so that they may become objects of knowledge and government' (book p. 26); 'a uniform enumeration would make a single Canadian population when in fact there were two' (book p. 98); 'demographic and social historians may ignore Curtis’ findings at their peril'; criticisms: the Nova Scotian and New Brunswick systems grafted on 'as though they were unproblematic', no bibliography, and 'deadening jargon' in the introduction and conclusion.

sources.scope_note: Near-period (2002) review; the witness to the census book's wording.

Inspection, Education, and State Formation in Canada West (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1992) and Allan Greer and Ian Radforth, eds., Colonial Leviathan: State Formation in Mid-Nineteenth Century Canada (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1992), Labour/Le Travail 31 (1993): 365–367 (in the issue's 'Reviews / Comptes Rendus' section, pp. 365–433).

verification.note: Read in full (pp. 365–367) in the journal's own PDF of the reviews section (lltjournal.ca article 4891, galley 5764; scanned pages with a text layer; folios 365, 366 and 367 printed in the running heads). Passages used: 'THESE BOOKS are searching for the state in pre-Confederation Canada'; 'In their purpose they can only be applauded; but their search is at times disturbingly narrow' (p. 365); Curtis 'telescopes the process of state formation in Canada West in the 1840s into the emergence of educational inspectors' and 'this study is too minutely focused' (p. 365); the promotional claim that Curtis 'presents a systematic application of the insights of ... Marx, Weber, Durkheim, Gramsci, and Foucault' (p. 365); as a 'model' Curtis's account 'is overstated to the point of distorting actual historical relations in the evolution of state and civil society' (p. 366); 'the collection lacks coherence' (p. 366); 'The single most important contribution of the articles in this collection, also developed by Curtis, is the notion that the coming of ‘responsible government’ actually entailed the subversion of the reform strategy of the 1830s' (p. 366); the gender essays read as 'complementary to the revisionist assessment of ‘responsible government’ as an expression of a slight [sic] of hand that promised popular sovereignty at the same time as it delivered institutionalized subordination and regulation' (pp. 366–367); 'Books like these make the job easier' (p. 367). sources.title: Allan Greer, "Settler Colonialism and Beyond," Journal of the Canadian Historical Association / Revue de la Société historique du Canada 30, no. 1 (2019): 61–86.
sources.citation: Allan Greer, "Settler Colonialism and Beyond," Journal of the Canadian Historical Association / Revue de la Société historique du Canada 30, no. 1 (2019): 61–86.

verification.note: Abstract read: the settler approach has much to offer, but across 500 years of invading Indigenous North America the settler variety dominates some periods and regions and fades in others. 'Imperial/Commercial Penetration' and 'Extractivism' are other modes; extractivism has become predominant in recent decades. Addendum 2026-10-14: Read in full for the 1.139 Allan Greer person entry (Érudit PDF served to an ordinary request; text layer; folios 61–79, notes 80–86). Based on a keynote address to the CHA annual meeting (first-page note). Passages used: settler colonial theory 'does indeed have much to offer historians' but 'the settler variety stands out as a dominant force in some periods and regions, but it fades to insignificance in others' (p. 62); 'The late Patrick Wolfe, still the most important theorist of settler colonialism' (p. 62); the hazard of 'temporal flattening' 'when settler colonialism is casually invoked in ways that suggest a transhistorical, always-already quality, as though the settler-colonial condition had no discernible beginning and as if it could never end' (p. 63); 'Let me assure you that I am not here to trash or dismiss settler-colonial theory. I personally think it has a great deal to offer anyone trying to understand the present and the past of a country such as Canada' (p. 63); historians 'need to take on board the critique of settler-national historiography sketched out by Wolfe and developed more fully by others such as Lorenzo Veracini' (p. 63); 'However, that doesn't mean we need to find settler colonialism everywhere and all the time' (p. 63); 'My objective is to try to historicize settler colonialism' (p. 63); 'Imperial/Commercial Penetration' and 'Extractivism' as 'coexisting and overlapping versions of colonialism' (p. 64); early settlements 'hardly functioned as instruments of elimination and replacement except in quite limited, localized ways' (p. 64); settler colonization 'emerged as an important independent force' only from the last quarter of the eighteenth century (p. 70); 'The time may be right, then, for a renewed history of the Confederation era, one that unites the history of state formation with that of settler colonialism' (p. 73), with n. 41: 'A prime example of this problem would be Colonial Leviathan; devoted to questions of state formation, it neglected everything to do with Indigenous peoples and processes of elimination' (p. 84); 'To those who insist that Canada is, was, and always has been a settler-colonial phenomenon, I offer qualified support' (p. 73); 'settlers as such are no longer the main threat, for the invasion has adopted a different guise' (p. 74); 'Settler colonialism stands out also as a fundamental force behind the creation of a territorial nation-state' and 'An order based on territorial dispossession is not, and never has been, normal, natural, and inevitable' (p. 79). The source's page range 61–86 includes the notes.
